intro: A flourish, a silence, then a chord built from the bottom up: the organ makes a theatre of the opening. Norbert Schenk plays the complete Toccata and Fugue at the Evangelische Kirche in Solms-Albshausen.

cues.title: A flourish, then silence
cues.text: The organ’s opening line bites into its first note, pauses, then plunges down in octaves. A low D remains underneath as a dissonant chord climbs into place, note by note.
cues.evidence: Opening of BWV 565: octave doubling, mordent and diminished-seventh chord over D. Netherlands Bach Society: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-565. Harmonic description: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fugue keeps running
cues.text: The fugue’s subject is made entirely of semiquavers. It keeps coming back to a fixed note while a second line seems to fall and rise around it. As other voices take up the subject, the organ turns that single line into a conversation.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, fugue subject and exposition; the implied pedal note and melodic line are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Johannes Ringk’s copy
cues.text: The earliest surviving copy bears the name of Johannes Ringk. On its title page he writes Toccata con Fuga and names Bach; inside, the pedal part shares the keyboard staves. Little letters tell the organist when the feet take over.
cues.evidence: Johannes Ringk manuscript, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 595; pedal notes marked p. The copy’s date is disputed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565

cues.title: The organ speaks freely
cues.text: The closing section breaks out of the fugue’s steady semiquavers. The marking is Recitativo: the organ speaks in runs, pauses and broad chords. Several changes of speed lead towards the final Molto adagio and its D-minor close.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, seventeen-bar coda, marked Recitativo and ending Molto adagio with a minor plagal cadence. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education.

In 1703 Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and married his second cousin Maria Barbara. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
